ev.rus_fc_caul.amulet.ok: The caul was dried on the stove, sewn into a little linen bag and hung round your neck. The midwife said never to take it off – except in the bathhouse.
ev.rus_fc_caul.threshold.ok: The caul was buried under the threshold with a muttered charm to keep luck from leaving the yard. For days the neighbour women dropped by to look at the "lucky" baby.
ev.rus_fc_caul.burn.ok: "Luck is in your hands, not in films," your grandfather grumbled, and the caul went into the stove. The midwife pursed her lips but did not argue.
ev.rus_fc_caul.title: Born with a caul
ev.rus_fc_caul.text: You were born in the bathhouse, and not just anyhow – with a caul, a thin film over your head. The old midwife threw up her hands: "A lucky one! Fire won't burn this child, water won't drown it!" The caul can be dried and sewn into a pouch to wear round the neck, or buried under the threshold so that luck stays with the whole house.
ev.rus_fc_caul.note: To be "born with a caul" is to come into the world inside the birth membrane, or with a piece of it over the head. Folk belief held that such a child would be lucky, and the caul was kept as a charm – sewn into a pouch or hidden in the house. Ethnographers recorded these customs later, but the belief was shared by many peoples of Europe.
ev.rus_fc_caul_ice.title: Thin ice
ev.rus_fc_caul_ice.text: The ice on the river cracked right under you, and you went down into the black water. How you got out you can't remember; on the bank the pouch round your neck was soaked through. Now the whole district says: "What do you expect – born with a caul."
ev.rus_fc_caul_yard.title: Luck stayed in the yard
ev.rus_fc_caul_yard.text: That year a cattle plague swept the district: the neighbours lost their beasts, but trouble passed your yard by. Old women nod at the threshold where your caul lies buried and bring you eggs or a pie "for luck". You laugh – but you step over that threshold with respect.
ev.rus_fc_names.secular.ok: So you had two names: one known to the priest and the calendar, the other to the whole street. Grandmother was satisfied: "Let evil go looking."
ev.rus_fc_names.church.ok: "A baptised child has nothing to hide from," your father decided. The priest praised his firmness and promised to keep an eye on you.
ev.rus_fc_names.title: Two names
ev.rus_fc_names.text: The priest baptised you and named you from the church calendar, after the saint whose feast fell in these days. Your grandmother whispers that it isn't enough: give the child a household name too – something like {g:Nezhdan|Nezhdana}, "the Unexpected" – so that evil searches by one name while people call by another. Your father hesitates: is it not a sin to hide a child from God?
ev.rus_fc_names.note: In Rus children were baptised by the church calendar, which lists the saints remembered on each day. But many people also had a second, worldly name – Zhdan, Nezhdan, Tretyak, Istoma. It was used in everyday life and sometimes even made its way into documents: "Ivan, by worldly name Tretyak". A double name, it was believed, confused the evil powers.
ev.rus_fc_names_fever.title: Evil looked elsewhere
ev.rus_fc_names_fever.text: In winter a fever went down the street: children took to their beds in several houses, and so did you. You pulled through, and grandmother is triumphant: "Evil called you by your baptismal name, but out here everyone shouts {g:Nezhdan|Nezhdana}! So it never found you."
ev.rus_fc_names_psalter.title: The priest's Psalter
ev.rus_fc_names_psalter.text: The priest who baptised you kept his promise: after services he began calling you in to learn your letters – first the alphabet, then the Psalter. You scratched the letters onto birch bark with a bone stylus, and by spring you could spell out a whole psalm.
